paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When we visit the centre of a large city anywhere in the world, we can become quickly overwhelmed by the sheer numbers of people moving around us, going about their daily business. The name we give to a situation where there appear to us to be too many people for a given space is 'crowding'. As the world's population increases, the number of people in cities can be expected to increase. By 1980 the world's population was over four billion, and in less than 40 years it will double again. One consequence of this population explosion is that people are living closer together and each person has less space to live in.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Recently, social scientists have begun to identify the consequences of living at increasingly smaller distances from other people. However, before we consider this research, it is important for us to understand the difference between two terms: density and crowding. Density is a measure of the space available to people in a given area. Crowding, on the other hand, is a psychological state rather than a physical measure. You can feel crowded, but you cannot 'feel' density. Density and crowding are often related but, as we will see later, this is not always the case.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In 1962, a researcher named John Calhoun published the results of a study that shocked social scientists and added a new urgency to the study of density and crowding. Calhoun built a rat colony with four rooms designed to hold about 48 animals. However, he let the population grow until it reached 80. The rats were given enough food, water and nesting material to maintain a high standard of living, but problems soon began to develop. Some dominant rats laid claim to two of the rooms, forcing the rest of the rats to live in the remaining two rooms. As a result of overcrowding. these two areas became behavioural sinks, which aggravated all forms of normally unacceptable social behaviour.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In response to Calhoun's experiment with the rat colony, a number of investigators then conducted studies comparing the behaviour of human individuals living in different densities. The results of these studies were interesting: some found bad effects (high rates of mental illness and juvenile delinquency) associated with high density, while others did not. Furthermore, even in the studies that reported negative behaviour related to high density, it was not possible to know for sure that high density was the cause of the problem. For example, the highest density areas are usually found in the inner cities, and residents of these are often poorer, less educated and have less job security than people living in the lower density suburbs.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: After an examination of the effects of density, researchers began to turn their attention to identifying the conditions under which high density leads to crowding, stress and behavioural effects. A number of factors have been found to influence the amount of crowding people will experience. First, the focus of our attention determines when we will feel crowded. When other people who are violating our personal space become the centre of our attention, we will attribute our arousal and discomfort to their closeness. This will result in our feeling crowded. For example, at an athletics event people's attention is focused on the competition and not on the other spectators: as a result, they are not likely to experience much crowding. But if the spectators are trying to leave the area after the event is over, they may experience crowding because they now see other people as preventing them from leaving as quickly as they would like to. Another area where high density may lead to crowding is when people feel that they have no control over their environment. The experience of a person in a packed department store can lead to feelings of utter helplessness; not only is it difficult to get to the cashier, but it is not possible to go against the flow of people moving into the store. Crowding is also likely to be felt when people cannot achieve the kind of privacy they want. Privacy means being able to choose whether or not to interact with others. When high density forces us to interact with others against our will, we may experience crowding.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: While high density by itself does not necessarily lead to negative reactions from people, the research on crowding presents a different picture. Crowding often has a negative impact on our emotions, performance and interpersonal relations. One common result is that we are less attracted to people in crowded than in non-crowded conditions. Interestingly enough, this effect has been consistently found for males but not for females. This may be due to the larger personal space areas (zones) that males have or else to a tendency for females to act co-operatively, while males are more likely to respond to others competitively. This may explain why there is often a high incidence of violence in male prisons. Also, in addition to tending toward aggression, people are less likely to help others in crowded, as opposed to non-crowded, environments.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The distinction between density and crowding also has some important implications for managing our environment. The first implication is that giving people more space will not necessarily reduce their sense of crowding. Secondly, crowding can be reduced without reducing density. For example, it was found that people who felt that they could easily leave a room full of people felt less crowded than people who thought it would be difficult to leave. Other research supporting this has found that people feel less crowded in high density environments if they have control. In another study, it was found that people felt less crowded and performed better in a room with pictures on the walls than in a room with no pictures, even though the density was the same in both situations. The investigators argued that the pictures made the presence of other people less obvious and thereby reduced crowding. Thus, there are many ways that crowding and its effects can be reduced without increasing space or decreasing the number of people in the environment.
